title: 1 · Mathematical Foundations
text:
Every later part averages some function of a random unitary, and to state what is being averaged one needs density matrices for the states, completely positive maps for the noisy evolutions, and a precise meaning for the word random. This part assembles that vocabulary from elementary pieces. The Lie algebras \(\mathfrak{u}(D)\) and \(\mathfrak{su}(D)\) are built from commutators and the matrix exponential, the geometry of pure states from the Fubini-Study metric, and the notion of a uniform distribution on \(U(D)\) from enough measure theory to make \(\sigma\)-additivity and measurability concrete. No prior exposure to Lie groups is assumed.
Two constructions do most of the later work. The Choi-Jamiołkowski isomorphism turns a quantum channel into a state on a doubled Hilbert space, converting questions about maps into questions about matrices. Schur-Weyl duality identifies the operators that commute with \(U^{\otimes k}\) for every \(U\) with the algebra generated by permutations of the \(k\) copies, which is why Haar averages over many entries collapse onto a small number of permutation terms. The notebooks work the \(k=2\) case in full, where the only operators in play are the identity and the SWAP.
One point deserves early emphasis. Closing a set of generators under repeated commutators produces the dynamical Lie algebra, and whether that algebra fills out all of \(\mathfrak{su}(D)\) or stays inside a subalgebra decides both whether a gate set is universal and how fast an operator can grow under the dynamics of later chapters.

title: 2 · Random Matrix Theory
text:
A quantum system with no integrable structure has energy levels that look erratic, yet their fine-grained statistics are reproducible. Across nuclei, quantum billiards, and disordered conductors, the spacing distribution of neighbouring levels matches that of a random matrix sharing the system’s symmetries, the content of the Bohigas-Giannoni-Schmit conjecture. Random matrix theory supplies the reference distributions and explains why they are universal.
The mechanism is level repulsion. Changing variables from matrix entries to eigenvalues produces a Jacobian carrying a factor of the squared eigenvalue differences, which suppresses configurations with near-degenerate levels. The power with which that factor vanishes is fixed by the time-reversal and spin-rotation symmetry of the ensemble, giving exponents \(1\), \(2\), and \(4\) for the orthogonal, unitary, and symplectic classes. This part derives the Wigner surmise from the two-by-two case, computes the semicircle density through its moments and the Catalan numbers that count them, and introduces the gap-ratio statistic that diagnoses chaos without the spectral unfolding that raw level spacings require.
One caution about the surmise. It is exact only for \(2\times2\) matrices; its accuracy at large dimension is an empirical near-coincidence rather than the true large-\(N\) spacing law. This is part of why the gap ratio, which is insensitive to the local mean level density, is often preferred in practice.

title: 3 · Haar Measure & Weingarten Calculus
text:
Most of the quantitative statements in this subject are averages over the unitary group. One asks for the mean of a polynomial in the entries of a random unitary, the entanglement of a state prepared by a random circuit, the variance of a cost-function gradient, the fidelity that survives a noisy gate. In each case the hard-looking object is a low moment of the Haar measure, the unique distribution on \(U(d)\) invariant under left and right multiplication. The Weingarten calculus is what turns these averages into arithmetic.
The mechanism rests on one representation-theoretic fact. Averaging \(k\) copies of \(U\) produces an operator that commutes with \(U^{\otimes k}\) for every \(U\), so it lies in the commutant of the \(k\)-fold representation. Schur-Weyl duality identifies that commutant with the algebra generated by permutations of the \(k\) tensor factors. An integral over a continuous group therefore collapses to a finite sum over the symmetric group \(S_k\), with coefficients supplied by the Weingarten function. For the second moment the only permutations are the identity and the swap, and a surprising amount of the later material follows from that single case.
Three consequences are worth isolating before the notebooks. The first moment is a twirl, sending any operator to its normalized trace times the identity, which is the precise sense in which a uniformly random rotation erases everything but the trace. The second moment produces purities, frame potentials, and the Page formula for the entanglement of a typical pure state. Concentration of measure then upgrades these averages from typical to overwhelming, so that in high dimension a single random state already behaves like the whole ensemble. The factor \(1/d\) that fixes the mean purity is the same one that reappears later as the variance of a barren-plateau gradient, which is the thread running from this part to quantum machine learning.

title: 3 · Haar Measure & Weingarten Calculus
text:
Notebooks in this part

The first Haar moment (twirling), averaging an operator to its normalized trace times the identity.
The SWAP trick, turning purity into a two-copy expectation value.
Overlaps of random states, the distribution of \(|\langle\psi|\phi\rangle|^2\) and its moments.
Fourth moment of the trace, a warm-up: \(\mathbb{E}|\mathrm{Tr}\,U|^4 = 2\).
Weingarten calculus as tensor networks, diagrammatic contractions, including the third trace moment.
The Page formula, average entanglement of a random state, via Marchenko-Pastur.
Concentration of purity, why a random subsystem is almost exactly maximally mixed.







The single most reused result in this tutorial is the second-moment twirl \(\mathbb{E}_U[U^{\otimes 2}\,X\,U^{\dagger\otimes 2}] = c_{\mathbb{I}}\,\mathbb{I} + c_{\mathbb{F}}\,\mathbb{F}\). If you internalize one calculation, make it this one.

title: 4 · Quantum Dynamics & Chaos
text:
Random matrix theory characterizes a chaotic spectrum but says nothing about how information moves in time. This part follows an operator that starts local and asks how it spreads across the system, the process called scrambling, and collects the diagnostics that detect it.
The out-of-time-ordered correlator is the primary probe. The squared commutator \(C(t) = \langle |[W(t), V]|^2\rangle\) measures the overlap that an initially distant operator \(W(t)\) develops with a fixed local \(V\), and its early growth defines a quantum Lyapunov exponent bounded by the Maldacena-Shenker-Stanford inequality \(\lambda \le 2\pi k_B T/\hbar\). The spectral form factor reads the same chaos off the spectrum directly; its dip, ramp, and plateau encode level repulsion in the time domain, with the plateau height pinned at the Hilbert-space dimension. Krylov complexity recasts operator growth in a basis-independent form, mapping the Heisenberg evolution onto a single particle hopping on a semi-infinite chain whose hopping amplitudes are the Lanczos coefficients.
It is worth keeping straight what each quantity sees. The squared commutator and the OTOC are tied by an exact identity at infinite temperature, so operator growth and a fidelity decay are two readings of one object, whereas the spectral form factor depends on the spectrum alone and is blind to the choice of operator.

Notebooks in this part

The spectral form factor, dip, ramp, and the plateau at \(K = D\).

title: 5 · Designs & Clifford Ensembles
text:
A Haar-random unitary on \(N\) qubits needs exponentially many real parameters to specify and cannot be sampled or stored efficiently. Most calculations, however, touch the Haar measure only through its low moments, the averages of \(U^{\otimes t} \otimes \bar U^{\otimes t}\). A unitary \(t\)-design is a finite ensemble that reproduces those averages up to order \(t\), which is all the randomness the second-moment and fourth-moment formulas of Parts 3 and 6 actually consume.
The Clifford group is the standard construction. It is an exact \(3\)-design and, by the Gottesman-Knill theorem, can be sampled and simulated classically in polynomial time. That same simulability marks what a design leaves out. Clifford circuits reach near-maximal entanglement, yet their out-of-time-ordered correlator takes only the values \(0\) and \(4\), with no smooth Lyapunov growth, so entanglement and genuine scrambling come apart here.
The missing resource is nonstabilizerness, or magic, the degree to which a state lies outside the set reachable by Clifford operations on computational basis states. The stabilizer Rényi entropy quantifies it from the expansion of the state over Pauli operators, vanishing exactly on stabilizer states and positive otherwise, and it is the quantity that separates a \(3\)-design from full Haar randomness.

title: 5 · Designs & Clifford Ensembles
text:
Notebooks in this part

Clifford OTOCs, why Clifford circuits scramble but have no Lyapunov exponent (the OTOC is \(0\) or \(4\)).
Stabilizer Rényi entropy, measuring “magic,” the resource beyond entanglement.

title: 6 · Applications of Scrambling
text:
In the earlier chapters randomness is something to characterize. Here it is deployed on purpose, because the same Haar second moment that fixes the Page curve also underwrites protocols for learning and benchmarking quantum systems and sharpens a thought experiment about black holes.
Classical shadows use random single-copy measurements followed by an analytic inversion of the measurement channel to predict many observables of an unknown state from few copies, with a sample cost controlled by a shadow norm that grows as \(3^k\) for \(k\)-local Pauli observables. Randomized benchmarking averages over random Clifford sequences so that gate-dependent noise twirls into a single depolarizing channel, whose strength is read from the exponential decay of the survival probability and reported as an average fidelity. Both rest on the same twirl, the second-moment average that replaces a complicated operator by a combination of the identity and the swap.
The Hayden-Preskill thought experiment applies that mathematics to a black hole modelled as a fast scrambler. Information dropped in can be reconstructed from the outgoing radiation almost as soon as it is absorbed, provided one already holds the radiation emitted earlier, a statement the decoupling theorem makes precise and which reuses the Page-curve estimate of Part 3. Tripartite mutual information turns the same average into a scrambling diagnostic, while the fragility of GHZ-state metrology shows the cost of storing information non-locally, where the loss of a single qubit erases a Heisenberg-scaling signal.

title: 7 · Quantum Machine Learning
text:
A variational quantum circuit is trained by following the gradient of a cost function, which works only when that gradient is large enough to estimate from a realistic number of measurements. Once the circuit is expressive enough to form an approximate \(2\)-design over its parameters, the Haar second moment from Part 3 forces the variance of every gradient component to shrink exponentially in the qubit count. This is the barren plateau, where the landscape is flat to within sampling noise and gradient-based optimization has no direction to follow.
The same second-moment estimate identifies what restores a usable gradient. Local cost functions, restricted symmetry sectors, and shallow circuit blocks all keep the ensemble short of a full \(2\)-design and recover a variance that decays only polynomially. The plateau reappears under other names with one origin. Quantum kernel entries concentrate around a fixed value and lose the structure a kernel method relies on, the quantum Fisher information matrix flattens in the metrology reading of the same collapse, and generative and reservoir models, from Born machines to extreme learning machines and reservoir computers, push their output distributions toward Porter-Thomas statistics so that the informative signal concentrates away.
The operative tension is that scrambling supplies expressivity while removing trainability, so the workable regime is a structured ensemble that stops short of Haar randomness.

title: 7 · Quantum Machine Learning
text:
Notebooks in this part

Barren plateaus, gradient variance vanishing exponentially with qubit number.
Local vs global cost functions, how observable locality rescues trainability.
Barren plateaus via quantum Fisher information, the metrology view of the same collapse.

Born-machine expressivity, concentration of a generative model’s output distribution.

Full circle. The exponential that obstructs training here is the same \(1/D\) from the Page formula in Part 3, typicality, viewed from the other side.

title: From Haar Random States to Quantum Machine Learning
text:
A recurring lesson in quantum many-body physics and quantum information is that the typical behaviour of a complex quantum system is sharply constrained, even when its microscopic details are not. Averages over the unitary group, known as the Haar measure, together with the concentration of measure that accompanies them, turn this observation into quantitative predictions. The same low-order Haar moments then reappear in settings that look, at first, unrelated.
The apparent thermality of a small subsystem follows from the entanglement of typical states. The recovery of information from an evaporating black hole is governed by the same Page-curve estimate of subsystem entropy. The protocols that certify quantum hardware, including randomized benchmarking, cross-entropy benchmarking and classical shadows, rest on second moments of the Haar measure. The trainability of variational quantum circuits, through the barren-plateau phenomenon, is fixed by the same concentration that renders typical states featureless.
The resemblance is not superficial. In each of these cases the underlying object is the same low-order average over the unitary group, evaluated in a different physical context. The technical core is correspondingly compact, consisting of Haar averaging, the Weingarten calculus and a modest amount of representation theory. This tutorial develops it once and applies it across each setting, with every step carried out explicitly and checked numerically.
Readers who want the mathematics in more depth can consult the companion lecture notes, Information Scrambling, Quantum Chaos, and Haar-Random States (arXiv:2511.14397), which these notebooks accompany.

title: Borel σ-Algebra and Measurability on U(D)
text:
This exercise bridges the abstract formalism of σ-algebras and measurable functions to the concrete quantum information quantities that we integrate against the Haar measure throughout the book. We verify that familiar functions, the survival probability \(|\langle 0|U|0\rangle|^2\) and the entanglement entropy \(S(\mathrm{Tr}_B[U|00\rangle\!\langle 00|U^\dagger])\), are Borel-measurable on the unitary group, and hence legitimate integrands for Haar averaging. The exercise also constructs the σ-algebra of the finite Pauli group to ground the abstract axioms in a hands-on computation.


Writing down an average of a function over the unitary group quietly assumes that the function can be integrated, and integration in turn requires the function to be measurable. Measurable means that the set of inputs landing in any chosen interval is one the measure knows how to weigh, that is, a Borel set. Without this property the integral that defines a Haar average would have no meaning, so measurability is the entry ticket for any quantity we want to average.
Continuous functions pass this test for free. A continuous function pulls every open set back to an open set, and the open sets are exactly what generate the Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra, so the preimage of any Borel set is again Borel. Since the quantities averaged over \(U(D)\) throughout the book depend continuously on the matrix entries of \(U\), each one is automatically a legitimate integrand and the averages are well posed.
In practice one checks measurability by breaking a function into continuous building blocks and using the fact that composing continuous maps stays continuous. The survival probability \(|\langle 0|U|0\rangle|^2\) is a polynomial in the entries of \(U\) and so is continuous outright. The entanglement entropy takes more steps, passing through a partial trace and then the continuous map \(-x\log x\) applied to the eigenvalues of the reduced state, yet each step preserves continuity. On a finite group like the Pauli group the question evaporates, because every subset belongs to the \(\sigma\)-algebra and so every function is measurable.
The notebook follows both functions through their continuous steps and contrasts them with the finite-group case.



Every time we write an expression like \[
\mathbb{E}_U\bigl[f(U)\bigr] = \int_{U(D)} f(U)\, d\mu_{\mathrm{Haar}}(U),
\] we are implicitly assuming that \(f\) is a measurable function on \(U(D)\), that is, a function whose domain and range are compatible with the σ-algebras in play. Without this property, the integral is undefined.
But what does ‘measurable function’ actually mean? And for the functions we care about, fidelities, entropies, OTOCs, cost function gradients, why are they measurable?
The short answer is: continuous functions are automatically measurable. For the functions in this book, measurability follows because they can be decomposed into a chain of continuous operations (matrix entry extraction → polynomial combination → eigenvalue computation → entropy evaluation). This exercise makes each step explicit.
The final part constructs the power-set σ-algebra of the finite Pauli group, showing that for finite groups the measurability question is trivial, every function is measurable, and only becomes nontrivial for continuous groups like \(U(D)\).



We first recall the key definitions (introduced in Section 1.13 and the companion exercise on Lebesgue/counting measures) and then add the tools specific to measurable functions.

Recall: \(\Omega\), \(\mathcal{F}\), \(\mu\), and what ‘measurable’ means.

\(\Omega\) is the sample space (e.g., \(U(D)\), \(\mathbb{R}\), or a finite group).
\(\mathcal{F}\) is a σ-algebra on \(\Omega\): a collection of subsets of \(\Omega\) closed under complements and countable unions. A subset \(A \subseteq \Omega\) is called measurable if \(A \in \mathcal{F}\), meaning we can assign it a well-defined size \(\mu(A)\). A non-measurable subset (\(A \notin \mathcal{F}\)) cannot be assigned any consistent size at all.
\(\mu: \mathcal{F} \to [0,\infty]\) is a measure, the size assignment. The triple \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\) is a measure space.

Tool 1, Borel σ-algebra. When \(\Omega\) is a topological space (i.e., it has a notion of ‘open sets’, for example, \(U(D)\) with the matrix-entry topology), the Borel σ-algebra \(\mathcal{B}(\Omega)\) is the smallest σ-algebra containing all open sets. It contains all open sets, all closed sets, all countable intersections of open sets, and so on. For the unitary group: \(\mathcal{F} = \mathcal{B}(U(D))\). This is the σ-algebra on which the Haar measure lives.

Tool 2, Measurable functions. A function \(f: \Omega \to \mathbb{R}\) is called Borel-measurable (or simply ‘measurable’) if it is compatible with the σ-algebras: for every Borel set \(B \subseteq \mathbb{R}\), the preimage \(f^{-1}(B) = \{\omega \in \Omega : f(\omega) \in B\}\) belongs to \(\mathcal{F}\). Equivalently, for every \(a \in \mathbb{R}\), the set \(\{\omega : f(\omega) \leq a\}\) is in \(\mathcal{F}\). This ensures that questions like ‘what is the probability that \(f(U)\) lies in \([0.3, 0.7]\)?’ have well-defined answers.

Tool 3, Continuous ⟹ measurable. If \(f: \Omega \to \mathbb{R}\) is continuous, then \(f\) is automatically Borel-measurable. The reason: continuous functions pull open sets back to open sets, and open sets are in \(\mathcal{B}(\Omega)\) by definition. This is the key fact that makes almost every function in quantum information measurable.

Tool 4, Composition rule. If \(f\) and \(g\) are both continuous (or both measurable), then the composition \(g \circ f\) is also continuous (or measurable). This lets us build complex measurable functions from simple ones by chaining operations.

Tool 5, Eigenvalue continuity. For an \(n \times n\) Hermitian matrix \(H\) with eigenvalues \(\lambda_1 \leq \cdots \leq \lambda_n\), each \(\lambda_k(H)\) is a continuous function of the matrix entries. This follows from the Weyl perturbation inequality: \(|\lambda_k(H) - \lambda_k(H')| \leq \|H - H'\|_{\mathrm{op}}\).

Tool 6, Partial trace. For a bipartite Hilbert space \(\mathcal{H}_A \otimes \mathcal{H}_B\), the partial trace \(\mathrm{Tr}_B[\hat{\rho}]\) has matrix entries that are sums of products of entries of \(\hat{\rho}\), i.e., the partial trace is a linear (hence continuous) map. Therefore \(U \mapsto \mathrm{Tr}_B[U|00\rangle\!\langle 00|U^\dagger]\) is continuous.

Tool 7, Power-set σ-algebra. For a finite set \(\Omega\) with \(|\Omega| = n\), the power set \(2^\Omega\) (the collection of all subsets) is trivially a σ-algebra with \(|2^\Omega| = 2^n\) elements. Every subset is measurable, every function is measurable. The nontrivial σ-algebra structure arises only for infinite/continuous spaces.




(a) Survival probability is Borel-measurable. For \(\Omega = U(2)\) and \(f(U) = |\langle 0|U|0\rangle|^2\), prove that \(f\) is Borel-measurable by showing it is a composition of continuous functions.
(b) Entanglement entropy is Borel-measurable. For \(U \in U(4)\), the entanglement entropy \(S(U) = -\mathrm{Tr}[\hat{\rho}_A \log \hat{\rho}_A]\) with \(\hat{\rho}_A = \mathrm{Tr}_B[U|00\rangle\!\langle 00|U^\dagger]\) is measurable. Trace through the chain: matrix entries → partial trace → eigenvalues → entropy.
(c) Power-set σ-algebra of \(\mathcal{P}_N\). On the Pauli group \(\mathcal{P}_N = \{I, X, Y, Z\}^{\otimes N}\) (ignoring phases), verify axioms (S1)-(S3) for \(2^{\mathcal{P}_N}\), and compute \(|2^{\mathcal{P}_N}|\) for \(N = 1, 2\).





We decompose \(f\) into a chain of two continuous maps: \[
U \xrightarrow{\text{step 1: extract entry}} U_{00} \xrightarrow{\text{step 2: squared modulus}} |U_{00}|^2
\]

Step 1: The map \(U \mapsto U_{00}\) extracts the \((0,0)\) entry of the matrix. This is a coordinate projection from \(\mathbb{C}^{D \times D}\) to \(\mathbb{C}\), a linear map, hence continuous.
Step 2: The map \(z \mapsto |z|^2 = z\bar{z}\) is a polynomial in \(\mathrm{Re}(z)\) and \(\mathrm{Im}(z)\): \(|z|^2 = (\mathrm{Re}\,z)^2 + (\mathrm{Im}\,z)^2\). Polynomials are continuous.

By the composition rule (Tool 4), \(f = |\cdot|^2 \circ \pi_{00}\) is continuous, hence Borel-measurable by Tool 3. \(\square\)



We decompose the entropy into a chain of four continuous operations: \[
U \xrightarrow{\text{(i)}} \hat{\rho} = U|00\rangle\!\langle 00|U^\dagger \xrightarrow{\text{(ii)}} \hat{\rho}_A = \mathrm{Tr}_B[\hat{\rho}] \xrightarrow{\text{(iii)}} (\lambda_1, \lambda_2) \xrightarrow{\text{(iv)}} S = -\sum_i \lambda_i \log \lambda_i
\]
Each step is continuous:

(i) \(U \mapsto U|00\rangle\!\langle 00|U^\dagger\): the entries of \(\hat{\rho}\) are \(\hat{\rho}_{ij} = U_{i0}\overline{U_{j0}}\), products of matrix entries, hence continuous (polynomials).
(ii) \(\hat{\rho} \mapsto \mathrm{Tr}_B[\hat{\rho}]\): partial trace is a linear map, each entry of \(\hat{\rho}_A\) is a sum of entries of \(\hat{\rho}\), hence continuous (Tool 6).
(iii) \(\hat{\rho}_A \mapsto (\lambda_1, \lambda_2)\): eigenvalues of a Hermitian matrix depend continuously on the matrix entries (Tool 5, Weyl inequality).
(iv) \((\lambda_1, \lambda_2) \mapsto -\sum_i \lambda_i \log \lambda_i\): the function \(h(x) = -x \log x\) is continuous on \([0,1]\) (with \(h(0) = 0\) by convention), so \(S = h(\lambda_1) + h(\lambda_2)\) is continuous.

By repeated application of the composition rule, \(S(U)\) is a continuous function of the matrix entries of \(U\), hence Borel-measurable. \(\square\)



For a finite set \(\Omega = \mathcal{P}_N\) with \(|\Omega| = 4^N\) elements, \(\mathcal{F} = 2^\Omega\) satisfies the three σ-algebra axioms:

(S1) \(\Omega \in 2^\Omega\): trivially, \(\Omega\) is a subset of itself.
(S2) If \(A \in 2^\Omega\), then \(\Omega \setminus A \in 2^\Omega\): every subset of a finite set is in its power set.
(S3) If \(A_1, A_2, \ldots \in 2^\Omega\), then \(\bigcup_k A_k \subseteq \Omega\), hence \(\bigcup_k A_k \in 2^\Omega\).

The number of elements: \(|2^{\mathcal{P}_N}| = 2^{4^N}\). - \(N = 1\): \(|2^{\mathcal{P}_1}| = 2^4 = 16\). - \(N = 2\): \(|2^{\mathcal{P}_2}| = 2^{16} = 65{,}536\).
Physical insight: For finite groups, every subset is measurable (it belongs to the σ-algebra), and every function is measurable. This is why the ‘average over Paulis’ \(\frac{1}{4^N}\sum_P f(P)\) never requires σ-algebra considerations. The nontrivial structure, which subsets are measurable and which are not, only appears for continuous groups like \(U(D)\).







Code
import sympy as sp

# ── Part (a): f(U) = |U₀₀|² is a polynomial ─────────────────────
# Show that f is a polynomial in Re(U₀₀) and Im(U₀₀),
# hence continuous → Borel-measurable.

x, y = sp.symbols('x y', real=True)  # x = Re(U₀₀), y = Im(U₀₀)
z = x + sp.I * y  # U₀₀ = x + iy

f_symbolic = sp.Abs(z)**2
f_expanded = sp.expand(sp.re(z * sp.conjugate(z)))
print(f'f(U) = |U₀₀|² = |x + iy|² = {f_expanded}')

# ── Part (b): Numerical continuity of S(U) on U(4) ───────────────
# Demonstrate each step of the chain is continuous.

D = 4  # Two qubits
ket_00 = np.zeros(D, dtype=complex)
ket_00[0] = 1.0

def entanglement_entropy(U):
    """S(Tr_B[U|00><00|U†]) - a measurable function on U(4).

    Chain of continuous operations:
      (i)   U → |ψ⟩ = U|00⟩ → ρ = |ψ⟩⟨ψ| (polynomial in U entries)
      (ii)  ρ → ρ_A = Tr_B(ρ)              (linear map)
      (iii) ρ_A → eigenvalues               (continuous by Weyl)
      (iv)  eigenvalues → S = -Σ λ log λ    (continuous on [0,1])
    """
    psi = U @ ket_00
    rho = np.outer(psi, psi.conj())
    rho_reshaped = rho.reshape(2, 2, 2, 2)
    rho_A = np.trace(rho_reshaped, axis1=1, axis2=3)
    eigs = np.linalg.eigvalsh(rho_A)
    eigs_pos = eigs[eigs > 1e-15]
    return float(-np.sum(eigs_pos * np.log(eigs_pos)))

title: Choi Matrix of the Amplitude-Damping Channel
text:
A quantum channel can be specified by listing its action on every input state, but that is an unwieldy object to test or compare. A tidier description packs the whole channel into one matrix. Prepare a maximally entangled pair, send one half through the channel while the other half waits untouched, and the joint state that comes out, the Choi matrix, encodes everything the channel can do. The Choi-Jamiolkowski isomorphism makes the dictionary between channel and matrix exact, and it trades a hard requirement for an easy one. Complete positivity, the demand that the channel stay physical even when applied to part of a larger entangled system, becomes the single statement that the Choi matrix has no negative eigenvalues.
The channel studied here is amplitude damping, which models an excited qubit leaking energy to its environment and settling toward its ground state. This is the \(T_1\) relaxation familiar from nuclear magnetic resonance and from superconducting qubits, where an excitation decays over time. Because every state is drawn toward \(|0\rangle\), the channel is non-unital and does not leave the maximally mixed state in place, unlike isotropic noise that has no preferred direction. A single parameter, the probability that the excitation is lost, sets how strong the damping is.
Reading the channel off its Choi matrix turns an abstract condition into a concrete calculation. Once the matrix is built, checking that it describes a valid channel is a matter of inspecting a four-by-four spectrum, and the rank of that matrix reports how many Kraus operators the channel genuinely needs, which in turn signals whether the channel is reversible or has begun to lose information.
This exercise builds the Choi matrix from the Kraus operators, finds its spectrum \(\{2-\gamma,\gamma,0,0\}\) and confirms that it stays non-negative for every damping strength, and reads the limiting cases of no damping and full reset off the rank of the matrix.



The amplitude-damping channel has Kraus operators
\[
K_0 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt{1-\gamma} \end{pmatrix}, \qquad
K_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & \sqrt{\gamma} \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix},
\]
where \(\gamma \in [0,1]\) is the damping probability.
(a) Construct the Choi matrix \(J(\mathcal{E}) = \sum_{j,k} \mathcal{E}(|j\rangle\langle k|) \otimes |j\rangle\langle k|\).
(b) Show the eigenvalues of \(J\) are \(\{2-\gamma,\, \gamma,\, 0,\, 0\}\). Verify \(J \geq 0\) for \(\gamma \in [0,1]\).
(c) Interpret the limiting cases \(\gamma = 0\) (identity) and \(\gamma = 1\) (reset to \(|0\rangle\)).





Before constructing the Choi matrix, we verify that the Kraus operators satisfy the trace-preservation condition \(\sum_\mu K_\mu^\dagger K_\mu = I\):
\[
K_0^\dagger K_0 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1-\gamma \end{pmatrix}, \qquad
K_1^\dagger K_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \gamma \end{pmatrix}.
\]
\[
K_0^\dagger K_0 + K_1^\dagger K_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = I. \quad \checkmark
\]



The Choi matrix lives on \(\mathbb{C}^2 \otimes \mathbb{C}^2\) and is constructed by applying the channel to one half of a maximally entangled state. Equivalently, we compute \(\mathcal{E}(|j\rangle\langle k|)\) for all basis elements and assemble:
\[
J = \sum_{j,k=0}^1 \mathcal{E}(|j\rangle\langle k|) \otimes |j\rangle\langle k|,
\]
where \(\mathcal{E}(\rho) = K_0 \rho K_0^\dagger + K_1 \rho K_1^\dagger\).
Computing each block:
\[
\mathcal{E}(|0\rangle\langle 0|) = K_0|0\rangle\langle 0|K_0^\dagger + K_1|0\rangle\langle 0|K_1^\dagger = |0\rangle\langle 0| + 0 = |0\rangle\langle 0|.
\]
\[
\mathcal{E}(|0\rangle\langle 1|) = \sqrt{1-\gamma}\,|0\rangle\langle 1|, \qquad \mathcal{E}(|1\rangle\langle 0|) = \sqrt{1-\gamma}\,|1\rangle\langle 0|.
\]
\[
\mathcal{E}(|1\rangle\langle 1|) = (1-\gamma)|1\rangle\langle 1| + \gamma|0\rangle\langle 0|.
\]
The last equation is the key: the \(K_1\) Kraus operator transfers population from \(|1\rangle\) to \(|0\rangle\) with probability \(\gamma\).
Assembling in the ordered basis \(\{|00\rangle, |01\rangle, |10\rangle, |11\rangle\}\):
\[
\boxed{J = \begin{pmatrix}
1 & 0 & 0 & \sqrt{1-\gamma} \\
0 & \gamma & 0 & 0 \\
0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\
\sqrt{1-\gamma} & 0 & 0 & 1-\gamma
\end{pmatrix}.}
\]



The Choi matrix is block-diagonal with respect to the subspaces \(\{|00\rangle, |11\rangle\}\) and \(\{|01\rangle, |10\rangle\}\).
The \(|01\rangle\) entry is simply \(\gamma\), and the \(|10\rangle\) entry is \(0\). These contribute eigenvalues \(\gamma\) and \(0\).
The \(2 \times 2\) block in the \(\{|00\rangle, |11\rangle\}\) sector is
\[
B = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & \sqrt{1-\gamma} \\ \sqrt{1-\gamma} & 1-\gamma \end{pmatrix}.
\]
Its trace and determinant:
\[
\mathrm{Tr}(B) = 2 - \gamma, \qquad \det(B) = 1 \cdot (1-\gamma) - (\sqrt{1-\gamma})^2 = 0.
\]
Since \(\det(B) = 0\) and \(\mathrm{Tr}(B) = 2-\gamma\), the eigenvalues of \(B\) are \(\{2-\gamma, 0\}\).
Full spectrum:
\[
\boxed{\mathrm{spec}(J) = \{2-\gamma,\; \gamma,\; 0,\; 0\}.}
\]
For \(\gamma \in [0,1]\): both \(2-\gamma \geq 1 > 0\) and \(\gamma \geq 0\), so \(J \geq 0\). This confirms complete positivity via the Choi theorem.



\(\gamma = 0\) (identity channel): Eigenvalues \(\{2, 0, 0, 0\}\), rank 1. The Choi matrix is \(J = 2|\Omega\rangle\langle\Omega|\) where \(|\Omega\rangle = (|00\rangle + |11\rangle)/\sqrt{2}\) is the maximally entangled state. A rank-1 Choi matrix is the hallmark of a unitary channel.
\(\gamma = 1\) (reset channel): Eigenvalues \(\{1, 1, 0, 0\}\), rank 2. The channel completely erases the input: \(\mathcal{E}(\rho) = |0\rangle\langle 0|\) for all \(\rho\). The two nonzero eigenvalues reflect the two Kraus operators needed.
The transition from rank 1 to rank 2 as \(\gamma\) increases from 0 reflects the onset of genuine decoherence, the channel can no longer be undone by a unitary.

import numpy as np

for gamma_val in [0.0, 0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 1.0]:
    K0 = np.array([[1, 0], [0, np.sqrt(1 - gamma_val)]], dtype=complex)
    K1 = np.array([[0, np.sqrt(gamma_val)], [0, 0]], dtype=complex)

    J = np.zeros((4, 4), dtype=complex)
    for j in range(2):
        for k in range(2):
            jk = np.zeros((2, 2), dtype=complex)
            jk[j, k] = 1.0
            Ejk = K0 @ jk @ K0.conj().T + K1 @ jk @ K1.conj().T
            anc = np.zeros((2, 2), dtype=complex)
            anc[j, k] = 1.0
            J += np.kron(Ejk, anc)

    evals = sorted(np.linalg.eigvalsh(J))
    expected = sorted([0, 0, gamma_val, 2 - gamma_val])
    assert np.allclose(evals, expected, atol=1e-12)
    assert all(e >= -1e-12 for e in evals)

    print(f"γ={gamma_val:.1f}: eigenvalues = [{', '.join(f'{e:.4f}' for e in evals)}]")

print("\nAll eigenvalues ≥ 0 for γ ∈ [0,1]: complete positivity confirmed.")

The Choi matrix of the amplitude-damping channel has spectrum \(\{2-\gamma,\, \gamma,\, 0,\, 0\}\), which stays non-negative for all \(\gamma \in [0,1]\), so the channel is completely positive. Its rank rises from one at \(\gamma = 0\) to two once damping sets in, marking the onset of irreversible decoherence.

title: The Depolarizing Channel
text:
Real qubits are disturbed by their surroundings, and a quantum channel is the bookkeeping that turns an ideal input state into the noisy output that actually emerges. Among the single-qubit channels the depolarizing one is the most symmetric. With some probability it leaves the state untouched, and otherwise it discards it in favor of the maximally mixed state, with no axis on the Bloch sphere singled out. Geometrically the Bloch vector keeps its direction and only shrinks, by the same factor whichever way it points, which is what makes the whole channel a one-parameter family.
That isotropy is why the channel serves as a reference point for noise. Any single-qubit channel, however biased its errors, can be averaged over the Clifford group in a procedure called twirling, and the average always comes out as a depolarizing channel with the same mean effect. Twirling washes out the directional detail and keeps the part of the error that survives randomization, so the depolarizing model stands in for a generic error once its orientation has been scrambled. This is the reason it sits at the center of randomized benchmarking and of estimates for error-correction thresholds.
To quantify the damage one needs a figure of merit, and a useful one is the entanglement fidelity, which sends half of a maximally entangled pair through the channel and asks how much of the original entanglement survives. It reports how well the channel preserves correlations with a held-back reference, going beyond what happens to each input state on its own.
This exercise writes the channel in its Pauli-Kraus form, checks that it is unital and that the Kraus operators are complete, and computes the entanglement fidelity, the overlap that survives when the channel acts on one half of a maximally entangled pair. The fidelity falls linearly to one quarter as the noise reaches full strength.



The single-qubit depolarizing channel is \(\mathcal{E}_p(\rho) = (1-p)\rho + (p/2)I\), with equivalent Kraus form:
\[
\mathcal{E}_p(\rho) = \left(1-\frac{3p}{4}\right)\rho + \frac{p}{4}\bigl(X\rho X + Y\rho Y + Z\rho Z\bigr).
\]
(a) Show that \(\mathcal{E}_p\) is unital: \(\mathcal{E}_p(I/2) = I/2\).
(b) Verify the Kraus completeness relation \(\sum_k K_k^\dagger K_k = I\).
(c) Compute the entanglement fidelity \(F_e = \langle\Phi^+|(\mathcal{E}_p \otimes \mathrm{id})|\Phi^+\rangle\) and show \(F_e = 1 - 3p/4\).





A channel is unital if it preserves the identity: \(\mathcal{E}(I) = I\). For the Pauli-Kraus form, we need to evaluate \(\sigma_j \cdot (I/2) \cdot \sigma_j\) for each Pauli \(\sigma_j \in \{X, Y, Z\}\).
Since each Pauli matrix is unitary (\(\sigma_j^\dagger \sigma_j = I\)), we have:
\[
\sigma_j \frac{I}{2} \sigma_j = \frac{1}{2}\sigma_j \sigma_j = \frac{I}{2}.
\]
Substituting into the channel:
\[
\mathcal{E}_p\!\left(\frac{I}{2}\right) = \left(1-\frac{3p}{4}\right)\frac{I}{2} + \frac{p}{4}\cdot 3 \cdot \frac{I}{2} = \frac{I}{2}\left(1-\frac{3p}{4}+\frac{3p}{4}\right) = \frac{I}{2}. \quad \checkmark
\]
Interpretation: Unitality means the channel preserves the maximally mixed state, it does not “cool” the system (unlike amplitude damping). The depolarizing channel adds noise symmetrically in all directions.



The Kraus operators are \(K_0 = \sqrt{1-3p/4}\,I\) and \(K_j = \sqrt{p/4}\,\sigma_j\) for \(j \in \{1,2,3\}\).
\[
\sum_k K_k^\dagger K_k = \left(1-\frac{3p}{4}\right)I + \frac{p}{4}\sum_{j=1}^3 \sigma_j^2 = \left(1-\frac{3p}{4}\right)I + \frac{3p}{4}I = I. \quad \checkmark
\]



The entanglement fidelity measures how well the channel preserves entanglement with a reference system. For a maximally entangled state \(|\Phi^+\rangle = (|00\rangle + |11\rangle)/\sqrt{2}\):
\[
F_e = \sum_k |\langle\Phi^+|(K_k \otimes I)|\Phi^+\rangle|^2.
\]
Using the identity \(\langle\Phi^+|(A \otimes I)|\Phi^+\rangle = \mathrm{Tr}(A)/2\):

\(K_0 = \sqrt{1-3p/4}\,I\): \(|\mathrm{Tr}(K_0)/2|^2 = (1-3p/4)\).
\(K_j = \sqrt{p/4}\,\sigma_j\): \(|\mathrm{Tr}(\sigma_j)/2|^2 = 0\) (Paulis are traceless).

\[
\boxed{F_e = 1 - \frac{3p}{4}.}
\]
At \(p = 0\) (no noise): \(F_e = 1\). At \(p = 1\) (full depolarization): \(F_e = 1/4\), the entanglement fidelity of the completely depolarizing channel and the minimum within the depolarizing family.

import sympy as sp

p = sp.Symbol('p', real=True, positive=True)
sx = sp.Matrix([[0,1],[1,0]])
sy = sp.Matrix([[0,-sp.I],[sp.I,0]])
sz = sp.Matrix([[1,0],[0,-1]])
I2 = sp.eye(2)

# Part (a): Unitality
rho = I2 / 2
result = (1 - sp.Rational(3,4)*p)*rho
for s in [sx, sy, sz]:
    result += (p/4) * s * rho * s
assert sp.simplify(result - rho) == sp.zeros(2)
print("Part (a): E_p(I/2) = I/2")

# Part (b): Completeness
completeness = (1 - sp.Rational(3,4)*p)*I2
for s in [sx, sy, sz]:
    completeness += (p/4) * s * s
assert sp.simplify(completeness - I2) == sp.zeros(2)
print("Part (b): Σ K†K = I")

# Part (c): Fe = 1 - 3p/4
Fe = 1 - sp.Rational(3,4)*p
print(f"Part (c): F_e = {Fe}")


Part (a): E_p(I/2) = I/2
Part (b): Σ K†K = I
Part (c): F_e = 1 - 3*p/4

import numpy as np

sx = np.array([[0,1],[1,0]], dtype=complex)
sy = np.array([[0,-1j],[1j,0]])
sz = np.array([[1,0],[0,-1]], dtype=complex)
I2 = np.eye(2, dtype=complex)
paulis = [sx, sy, sz]

phi_plus = np.array([1,0,0,1], dtype=complex) / np.sqrt(2)

for p_val in [0.0, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0]:
    # Apply channel to half of |Φ+⟩
    rho_out = np.zeros((4,4), dtype=complex)
    rho_in = np.outer(phi_plus, phi_plus.conj())

    # K0 ⊗ I
    K0 = np.sqrt(1 - 3*p_val/4) * I2
    K0_full = np.kron(K0, I2)
    rho_out += K0_full @ rho_in @ K0_full.conj().T

    for s in paulis:
        Kj = np.sqrt(p_val/4) * s
        Kj_full = np.kron(Kj, I2)
        rho_out += Kj_full @ rho_in @ Kj_full.conj().T

    Fe = (phi_plus.conj() @ rho_out @ phi_plus).real
    Fe_pred = 1 - 3*p_val/4

    print(f"p={p_val:.2f}: F_e = {Fe:.4f} (pred {Fe_pred:.4f})")
    assert np.isclose(Fe, Fe_pred)

print("\nAll assertions passed.")

All assertions passed.






The depolarizing channel is unital and trace-preserving, with entanglement fidelity \(F_e = 1 - 3p/4\) that falls linearly in the noise strength. At full depolarization \(p = 1\) the fidelity reaches its floor of \(1/4\).

title: Differential Geometry of Quantum State Space
text:
This exercise develops the Riemannian geometry of quantum state space from first principles, connecting the Fubini-Study metric, Berry phase, and quantum geometric tensor into a unified framework that underpins the trainability analysis of Part 7 and the metrology of quantum scrambling.


Physics does not see the overall phase of a quantum state, so two vectors that differ only by a phase describe the same physical situation. Removing that redundancy from the space of qubit states leaves the complex projective line \(\mathbb{CP}^1\), which is the familiar Bloch sphere. To do geometry on this space we need a way to measure distance between nearby states, and the right one is the Fubini-Study metric, built so that it ignores the phase that physics discards.
A single object packages this metric together with the geometry of how states respond to changing a parameter. It is the quantum geometric tensor, a Hermitian object whose real part is the Fubini-Study metric and whose imaginary part is the Berry curvature. The metric tells us how far apart two states are, while the Berry curvature records the geometric phase that accumulates when a state is carried around a loop in parameter space.
The diagonal of this tensor has a direct operational meaning, since it gives the quantum Fisher information. That quantity sets the ultimate precision for estimating a parameter through the Cramer-Rao inequality, and the same Fisher information later governs how easily variational circuits can be trained. For a qubit swept across the Bloch sphere the real part reproduces the metric of a sphere of radius \(1/2\), while the imaginary part integrates to the flux of a single monopole. The Fisher information read from the diagonal drops to zero when the driving axis lines up with the initial Bloch vector.
The notebook evaluates the quantum geometric tensor for a qubit over the Bloch sphere and separates its metric and curvature parts.



A quantum state \(|\psi\rangle\) lives in the Hilbert space \(\mathcal{H} \cong \mathbb{C}^D\), but physical observables are blind to the overall phase: \(|\psi\rangle\) and \(e^{i\alpha}|\psi\rangle\) represent the same physics. The true arena of quantum mechanics is therefore the projective Hilbert space \(\mathbb{CP}^{D-1}\), obtained by quotienting out the \(U(1)\) phase.
This quotient endows \(\mathbb{CP}^{D-1}\) with a natural Riemannian metric, the Fubini-Study metric, that provides a gauge-invariant notion of distance between quantum states. This metric is not merely an abstract mathematical structure: it appears directly as the Quantum Fisher Information (QFI) in parameter estimation, as the Fubini-Study speed in quantum dynamics, and as the quantum geometric tensor controlling Berry phases and adiabatic transport.
Understanding this geometry is essential for: - Quantum metrology: The QFI bounds the precision of parameter estimation via the Cramér-Rao bound. - Variational algorithms: The Fubini-Study metric determines the natural gradient on the variational manifold. - Scrambling diagnostics: The QFI concentration bounds the trainability of deep circuits (Part 7).



Tool 1, Quantum Geometric Tensor (QGT): For a family of states \(|\psi(\boldsymbol{\theta})\rangle\) parameterized by \(\boldsymbol{\theta} = (\theta_1, \ldots, \theta_p)\), the QGT is: \[
Q_{\mu\nu} = \langle \partial_\mu \psi | \partial_\nu \psi \rangle - \langle \partial_\mu \psi | \psi \rangle \langle \psi | \partial_\nu \psi \rangle.
\] Its real part is the Fubini-Study metric \(g_{\mu\nu}^{\mathrm{FS}} = \mathrm{Re}\, Q_{\mu\nu}\); its imaginary part is proportional to the Berry curvature \(F_{\mu\nu} = -2\, \mathrm{Im}\, Q_{\mu\nu}\).
Tool 2, Fubini-Study distance: For two pure states, \[
d_{\mathrm{FS}}(|\psi\rangle, |\phi\rangle) = \arccos |\langle \psi | \phi \rangle|.
\]
Tool 3, QFI and Cramér-Rao bound: \(F_Q(\theta) = 4\, g_{\theta\theta}^{\mathrm{FS}}\). For unitary encoding \(|\psi(\theta)\rangle = e^{-i\theta G}|\psi_0\rangle\): \(F_Q = 4\,\mathrm{Var}(G)\).
Tool 4, Berry connection: \(A_\mu = i\langle \psi | \partial_\mu \psi \rangle\); the Berry curvature \(F_{\mu\nu} = \partial_\mu A_\nu - \partial_\nu A_\mu\) governs geometric phases.
Tool 5, Sectional curvature: For \(X, Y \in \mathfrak{su}(D)\) with \(\langle X, Y \rangle = -\mathrm{Tr}(XY)\): \(K(X,Y) = \frac{1}{4}\|[X,Y]\|^2\).



(a) Fubini-Study metric for a qubit. Consider a qubit state \(|\psi(\theta, \phi)\rangle = \cos(\theta/2)|0\rangle + e^{i\phi}\sin(\theta/2)|1\rangle\). Compute the full QGT and show: \[ds^2_{\mathrm{FS}} = \frac{1}{4}\left(d\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta\, d\phi^2\right).\]
(b) Berry curvature as monopole. Extract \(F_{\theta\phi}\) and show it corresponds to a magnetic monopole. Compute the total Berry flux and Chern number.
(c) QFI for a rotation. For \(|\psi(\theta)\rangle = e^{-i\theta \sigma_z/2}|+\rangle\), verify \(F_Q = 4\,\mathrm{Var}(\sigma_z/2) = 1\).
(d) QFI for general SU(2). Show \(F_Q = 1 - (\hat{n} \cdot \langle \boldsymbol{\sigma} \rangle_0)^2\). When does \(F_Q\) vanish?
(e) Geodesic distances. Compute \(d_{\mathrm{FS}}(|0\rangle, |+\rangle)\) and \(d_{\mathrm{FS}}(|0\rangle, |1\rangle)\).





Derivatives: \(|\partial_\theta \psi\rangle = (-\sin(\theta/2)/2)|0\rangle + (\cos(\theta/2)/2)e^{i\phi}|1\rangle\), \(|\partial_\phi \psi\rangle = i\sin(\theta/2)e^{i\phi}|1\rangle\).

\(Q_{\theta\theta} = 1/4\) (real, since \(\langle\psi|\partial_\theta\psi\rangle = 0\)).
\(Q_{\phi\phi} = \sin^2(\theta/2)\cos^2(\theta/2) = \sin^2\theta/4\) (real).
\(Q_{\theta\phi} = i\cos(\theta/2)\sin(\theta/2)/2 = i\sin\theta/4\) (purely imaginary \(\Rightarrow g_{\theta\phi} = 0\)).

The FS metric gives \(ds^2 = \frac{1}{4}(d\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta\,d\phi^2)\): the round sphere of radius \(R = 1/2\). \(\checkmark\)



\(F_{\theta\phi} = -2\,\mathrm{Im}\, Q_{\theta\phi} = -2 \cdot \sin\theta/4 = -\sin\theta/2\).
Total flux: \(\Phi = \int_0^{2\pi}d\phi \int_0^\pi d\theta\,(-\sin\theta/2) = -2\pi\). Chern number \(c_1 = \Phi/(2\pi) = -1\) for spin-\(\downarrow\). The magnitude \(|\Phi| = 2\pi\) confirms a monopole of strength \(1/2\).



For \(G = \sigma_z/2\) on \(|+\rangle\): \(\langle G\rangle = 0\), \(\langle G^2\rangle = 1/4\), so \(F_Q = 4(1/4 - 0) = 1\).
General: \(G = \hat{n}\cdot\boldsymbol{\sigma}/2\), \(G^2 = I/4\), \(\langle G\rangle = \hat{n}\cdot\langle\boldsymbol{\sigma}\rangle_0/2\). Therefore \(F_Q = 1 - (\hat{n}\cdot\langle\boldsymbol{\sigma}\rangle_0)^2\). Vanishes when \(|\psi_0\rangle\) is eigenstate of \(G\) (\(\hat{n}\) aligned with Bloch vector).



\(d_{\mathrm{FS}}(|0\rangle, |+\rangle) = \arccos(1/\sqrt{2}) = \pi/4\), \(d_{\mathrm{FS}}(|0\rangle, |1\rangle) = \arccos(0) = \pi/2\).

import numpy as np

def qubit_state(theta, phi):
    return np.array([np.cos(theta/2), np.exp(1j*phi)*np.sin(theta/2)])

def numerical_qgt(theta, phi, eps=1e-6):
    psi = qubit_state(theta, phi)
    dt = (qubit_state(theta+eps, phi) - qubit_state(theta-eps, phi)) / (2*eps)
    dp = (qubit_state(theta, phi+eps) - qubit_state(theta, phi-eps)) / (2*eps)
    derivs = [dt, dp]
    Q = np.zeros((2,2), dtype=complex)
    for i in range(2):
        for j in range(2):
            Q[i,j] = np.vdot(derivs[i], derivs[j]) - np.vdot(derivs[i], psi) * np.vdot(psi, derivs[j])
    return Q

theta = np.linspace(0, np.pi, 400)
g_tt = np.full_like(theta, 0.25)      # g_{theta theta} = 1/4
g_pp = np.sin(theta) ** 2 / 4         # g_{phi phi} = sin^2(theta)/4
F_tp = -np.sin(theta) / 2             # Berry curvature F_{theta phi}

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 4.0))
ax.plot(theta, g_tt, color='navy', lw=2, label=r'$g_{\theta\theta}=1/4$')
ax.plot(theta, g_pp, color='seagreen', lw=2,
        label=r'$g_{\phi\phi}=\sin^2\theta/4$')
ax.plot(theta, F_tp, color='crimson', lw=2,
        label=r'$F_{\theta\phi}=-\sin\theta/2$')
ax.axhline(0.0, color='gray', lw=0.7)
ax.set_xlabel(r'polar angle $\theta$')
ax.set_ylabel('tensor component')
ax.set_title('Quantum geometric tensor and Berry curvature of a qubit')
ax.set_xticks([0, np.pi / 2, np.pi])
ax.set_xticklabels(['0', r'$\pi/2$', r'$\pi$'])
ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()








The qubit quantum geometric tensor has real part \(\mathrm{diag}(1/4,\sin^2\theta/4)\), the Fubini-Study metric of a sphere of radius \(1/2\), and imaginary part the Berry curvature \(-\sin\theta/2\), whose total flux gives the Chern number \(-1\). The quantum Fisher information \(F_Q=1-(\hat n\cdot\langle\boldsymbol\sigma\rangle_0)^2\) vanishes exactly when the generator’s axis aligns with the initial Bloch vector.

title: Dimension of the Lie Algebras and
text:
Every continuous evolution of a \(D\)-dimensional quantum system is generated by a Hermitian Hamiltonian, and pulling out the factor of \(i\) turns these generators into skew-Hermitian matrices, the elements of the Lie algebra \(\mathfrak{u}(D)\). Keeping only the traceless ones gives \(\mathfrak{su}(D)\), the algebra attached to the special unitary group, whose elements generate the unitaries of unit determinant. Asking how large this algebra is amounts to asking how many independent generators it holds, which comes down to counting the real parameters left once the defining constraints are imposed.
The counting is direct. Skew-Hermiticity ties each below-diagonal entry to its mirror image above and forces every diagonal entry to be purely imaginary, so the free real parameters number \(D^2\). Requiring the trace to vanish removes exactly one more, since that is a single condition on the imaginary diagonal, leaving \(D^2 - 1\) generators for \(\mathfrak{su}(D)\). For a single qubit this recovers the three Pauli generators, as it should.
What matters is how the count grows with system size. For \(N\) qubits the dimension is \(D = 2^N\), and the generator count becomes \(4^N - 1\), an exponential in the number of qubits. The space of directions a generic circuit can move in is therefore enormous, and that very abundance is what dilutes the signal in variational optimization. When a circuit randomizes enough to imitate the first two moments of the unitary group, the variance of a cost-function gradient shrinks like \(4^{-N}\), and the training landscape flattens into a barren plateau where the gradients are too small to follow.
This exercise carries out the parameter count for \(\mathfrak{u}(D)\) and \(\mathfrak{su}(D)\), confirms the \(4^N - 1\) scaling for qubits, and connects it to the barren plateau.



(a) Count the real degrees of freedom in a \(D \times D\) skew-Hermitian matrix and show \(\dim_\mathbb{R}\, \mathfrak{u}(D) = D^2\).
(b) The tracelessness constraint \(\mathrm{Tr}(X) = 0\) defines \(\mathfrak{su}(D) \subset \mathfrak{u}(D)\). Show \(\dim_\mathbb{R}\, \mathfrak{su}(D) = D^2 - 1\).
(c) For \(N\) qubits (\(D = 2^N\)), how does \(\dim\,\mathfrak{su}(D)\) scale with \(N\)? Relate to the barren plateau phenomenon.





The Lie algebra \(\mathfrak{u}(D)\) consists of all skew-Hermitian matrices: \(X = -X^\dagger\). This constraint relates entries pairwise.
Diagonal entries (\(X_{jj}\)): The constraint \(X_{jj} = -\overline{X_{jj}}\) forces each diagonal entry to be purely imaginary: \(X_{jj} = i\theta_j\) with \(\theta_j \in \mathbb{R}\). This gives \(D\) real parameters.
Off-diagonal entries (\(j < k\)): The upper triangle has \(D(D-1)/2\) complex entries, each with 2 real parameters. The lower triangle is determined by \(X_{kj} = -\overline{X_{jk}}\). This gives \(D(D-1)\) real parameters.
Total:
\[
\boxed{\dim_\mathbb{R}\,\mathfrak{u}(D) = D + D(D-1) = D^2.}
\]



The special unitary algebra \(\mathfrak{su}(D)\) imposes the additional constraint \(\mathrm{Tr}(X) = 0\). Since
\[
\mathrm{Tr}(X) = \sum_{j=1}^D X_{jj} = i\sum_{j=1}^D \theta_j,
\]
the trace vanishes if and only if \(\sum_j \theta_j = 0\). This is a single real constraint on the \(D\) imaginary diagonal parameters. The off-diagonal entries are unaffected.
\[
\boxed{\dim_\mathbb{R}\,\mathfrak{su}(D) = D^2 - 1.}
\]
This matches the familiar count: \(\mathrm{SU}(2)\) has \(4 - 1 = 3\) generators (the Pauli matrices).



For \(N\) qubits, \(D = 2^N\) and
\[
\dim\,\mathfrak{su}(2^N) = 4^N - 1.
\]
This exponential growth has a direct physical consequence: the gradient variance in a variational quantum circuit that forms a 2-design scales as
\[
\mathrm{Var}\!\left[\frac{\partial C}{\partial\theta}\right] = O\!\left(\frac{1}{4^N}\right).
\]
The gradient is exponentially small because the cost function “lives” on a manifold with \(4^N - 1\) dimensions, the gradient signal is spread over an exponentially large space. This is the barren plateau phenomenon.







Code
import sympy as sp

D = sp.Symbol('D', positive=True, integer=True)

dim_uD = D**2
dim_suD = D**2 - 1

# Verify by components
diag_params = D
off_diag_params = D*(D-1)
total = sp.expand(diag_params + off_diag_params)
print(f"Diagonal: {diag_params}, Off-diagonal: {off_diag_params}")
print(f"Total: {total} = D² = {sp.expand(D**2)}")
assert total == D**2
print(f"dim u(D) = {dim_uD}, dim su(D) = {dim_suD}")


Diagonal: D, Off-diagonal: D*(D - 1)
Total: D**2 = D² = D**2
dim u(D) = D**2, dim su(D) = D**2 - 1








Code
import numpy as np

for D_val in [2, 4, 8, 16]:
    # Generate a random skew-Hermitian matrix
    A = np.random.randn(D_val, D_val) + 1j*np.random.randn(D_val, D_val)
    X = (A - A.conj().T) / 2  # Project to skew-Hermitian

    # Verify skew-Hermiticity
    assert np.allclose(X, -X.conj().T)

    # Count real parameters
    dim_u = D_val**2
    dim_su = D_val**2 - 1
    N_qubits = int(np.log2(D_val))

    print(f"D={D_val:3d} ({N_qubits}q): dim u(D) = {dim_u:6d}, "
          f"dim su(D) = {dim_su:6d} = 4^{N_qubits}−1 = {4**N_qubits - 1}")
    assert dim_su == 4**N_qubits - 1

print("\nExponential growth: dim su(2^N) = 4^N − 1.")


D=  2 (1q): dim u(D) =      4, dim su(D) =      3 = 4^1−1 = 3
D=  4 (2q): dim u(D) =     16, dim su(D) =     15 = 4^2−1 = 15
D=  8 (3q): dim u(D) =     64, dim su(D) =     63 = 4^3−1 = 63
D= 16 (4q): dim u(D) =    256, dim su(D) =    255 = 4^4−1 = 255

Exponential growth: dim su(2^N) = 4^N − 1.






Skew-Hermiticity gives \(\dim_\mathbb{R}\,\mathfrak{u}(D) = D^2\), and the single tracelessness constraint gives \(\dim_\mathbb{R}\,\mathfrak{su}(D) = D^2 - 1\). For \(N\) qubits this is \(4^N - 1\), the exponentially large manifold over which variational gradients are spread in a barren plateau.




Goodman and Wallach, Symmetry, Representations, and Invariants, Springer (2009).
Larocca et al., Barren plateaus in variational quantum computing, Nature Reviews Physics (2025).

title: The Adjoint Representation and DLA Closure
text:
A quantum circuit can switch on only the few Hamiltonians built into its hardware, yet by composing them over time it reaches a much larger set of unitaries. Which unitaries are within reach has a clean answer through the algebra the generators produce. Take each available Hamiltonian, multiply it by \(-i\) so that it generates a unitary flow, and close the collection under the commutator, adding every bracket of operators already present until nothing new appears. The span that results is the dynamical Lie algebra, the tangent space to the group of reachable unitaries, and its dimension counts the independent directions the circuit can steer in.
When the generators share a symmetry, the algebra cannot grow to fill the whole space of traceless generators \(\mathfrak{su}(D)\). The reason is short. Any operator that commutes with every generator also commutes with every commutator built from them, hence with the entire algebra. Such a conserved operator splits the Hilbert space into its eigenspaces, and the reachable unitaries leave each of those sectors in place rather than mixing them. The algebra is then block diagonal, and the directions that would carry one sector into another are simply missing.
This is the mechanism behind controllability and its failure. A circuit whose generators close onto all of \(\mathfrak{su}(D)\) can approximate any unitary, while a hidden conservation law confines it to a smaller reachable set, with consequences for what such a circuit can compute or simulate. Counting the dimension of the algebra is therefore a way to read off how much of the unitary group the hardware can actually access.
This exercise closes the algebra of the two-qubit transverse-field Ising generators by iterating commutators until no new operators appear, finds a six-dimensional algebra inside the fifteen-dimensional \(\mathfrak{su}(4)\), and identifies the parity operator \(\sigma_z\otimes\sigma_z\) as the conserved quantity that forbids the nine remaining directions.



Consider the 2-qubit transverse-field Ising generators:
\[
H_1 = \sigma_z \otimes I, \qquad H_2 = I \otimes \sigma_z, \qquad H_3 = \sigma_x \otimes \sigma_x.
\]
(a) Compute the commutator \([-iH_1, -iH_3]\) and express it in terms of Pauli tensor products.
(b) Starting from \(\{-iH_1, -iH_2, -iH_3\}\), iterate all nested commutators until the algebra closes. Show \(\dim(\mathrm{DLA}) = 6\).
(c) Verify that \(\sigma_z \otimes \sigma_z\) commutes with all three generators. This \(\mathbb{Z}_2\) parity symmetry restricts the DLA to a proper subalgebra of \(\mathfrak{su}(4)\).





We compute \([-iH_1, -iH_3]\). Using the identity \([-iA, -iB] = -[A, B]\):
\[
[H_1, H_3] = [\sigma_z \otimes I,\; \sigma_x \otimes \sigma_x].
\]
For tensor products, \([A \otimes B, C \otimes D] = [A,C] \otimes BD\) when \([B,D] = 0\) and \(\{B,D\} = 2BD\), but more generally we use the identity:
\[
[A \otimes B, C \otimes D] = AC \otimes BD - CA \otimes DB.
\]
Here \(B = I\) commutes with everything, so:
\[
[H_1, H_3] = [\sigma_z, \sigma_x] \otimes I \cdot \sigma_x = [\sigma_z, \sigma_x] \otimes \sigma_x.
\]
Using the Pauli commutation relation \([\sigma_z, \sigma_x] = -2i\sigma_y\):
\[
[-iH_1, -iH_3] = -[H_1, H_3] = 2i\,\sigma_y \otimes \sigma_x.
\]
This produces a new generator \(\sigma_y \otimes \sigma_x\) not in the original set.



We continue taking commutators of existing generators with each other until no new independent elements appear. Starting from \(\{-i\sigma_z I,\, -iI\sigma_z,\, -i\sigma_x\sigma_x\}\) and the new \(-i\sigma_y\sigma_x\):
The process generates (up to normalization) the six independent Pauli strings:
\[
\{\sigma_z I,\; I\sigma_z,\; \sigma_x\sigma_x,\; \sigma_y\sigma_x,\; \sigma_x\sigma_y,\; \sigma_y\sigma_y\}.
\]
All further commutators yield linear combinations of these six elements. Therefore:
\[
\boxed{\dim(\mathrm{DLA}) = 6.}
\]
Since \(\dim\,\mathfrak{su}(4) = 15\), the circuit can only explore a \(6\)-dimensional submanifold of the full 15-dimensional unitary group. Nine directions in \(\mathfrak{su}(4)\) are inaccessible, these correspond to operators that break the \(\mathbb{Z}_2\) parity symmetry.



The parity operator \(P = \sigma_z \otimes \sigma_z\) satisfies:
\[
[P, \sigma_z \otimes I] = 0, \qquad [P, I \otimes \sigma_z] = 0, \qquad [P, \sigma_x \otimes \sigma_x] = 0.
\]
The first two are immediate since \([\sigma_z, \sigma_z] = 0\). For the third: \(P \cdot H_3 = (\sigma_z\sigma_x) \otimes (\sigma_z\sigma_x) = (i\sigma_y)\otimes(i\sigma_y) = -\sigma_y\sigma_y\), and \(H_3 \cdot P = (\sigma_x\sigma_z)\otimes(\sigma_x\sigma_z) = (-i\sigma_y)(-i\sigma_y) = -\sigma_y\sigma_y\), so \([P, H_3] = 0\).
Since \(P\) commutes with all generators, by Schur’s lemma the Hilbert space decomposes into parity sectors \((P = +1\) and \(P = -1)\), and the DLA cannot connect them. This is why \(\dim(\mathrm{DLA}) = 6 < 15\).







Code
import sympy as sp
from sympy import Matrix, I, sqrt, simplify, trace

# Verify DLA closure for su(2): [sigma_i/2, sigma_j/2] = i*eps_{ijk}*sigma_k/2
sx = Matrix([[0, 1], [1, 0]])
sy = Matrix([[0, -I], [I, 0]])
sz = Matrix([[1, 0], [0, -1]])

# Generators g_k = -i*sigma_k/2 (Hermitian representation of su(2))
gx = -I * sx / 2
gy = -I * sy / 2
gz = -I * sz / 2

# Verify [gx, gy] = gz  (i.e., the Lie bracket closes)
comm_xy = simplify(gx * gy - gy * gx)
print(f'[gx, gy] = {comm_xy}')
print(f'gz       = {gz}')
assert comm_xy == gz, 'DLA closure failed!'
print('DLA closure [gx,gy]=gz verified!')

# Verify cyclic: [gy, gz] = gx, [gz, gx] = gy
assert simplify(gy * gz - gz * gy) == gx
assert simplify(gz * gx - gx * gz) == gy
print('[gy,gz]=gx and [gz,gx]=gy verified!')

# Dimension of su(n) = n^2 - 1
n = sp.Symbol('n', positive=True, integer=True)
dim_sun = n**2 - 1
print(f'\ndim(su(n)) = {dim_sun}')
for k in [2, 3, 4]:
    print(f'  su({k}): dim = {k**2-1}')


[gx, gy] = Matrix([[-I/2, 0], [0, I/2]])
gz       = Matrix([[-I/2, 0], [0, I/2]])
DLA closure [gx,gy]=gz verified!
[gy,gz]=gx and [gz,gx]=gy verified!

dim(su(n)) = n**2 - 1
  su(2): dim = 3
  su(3): dim = 8
  su(4): dim = 15








Code
import numpy as np

I2 = np.eye(2, dtype=complex)
sx = np.array([[0,1],[1,0]], dtype=complex)
sy = np.array([[0,-1j],[1j,0]])
sz = np.array([[1,0],[0,-1]], dtype=complex)

H1 = np.kron(sz, I2)
H2 = np.kron(I2, sz)
H3 = np.kron(sx, sx)

# DLA closure algorithm
basis = [-1j*H1, -1j*H2, -1j*H3]

def is_independent(new, basis, tol=1e-10):
    if len(basis) == 0:
        return True
    mat = np.array([b.flatten() for b in basis])
    vec = new.flatten()
    # Project out existing basis components
    for row in mat:
        vec = vec - np.dot(row.conj(), vec) / np.dot(row.conj(), row) * row
    return np.linalg.norm(vec) > tol

changed = True
while changed:
    changed = False
    for i in range(len(basis)):
        for j in range(i+1, len(basis)):
            comm = basis[i] @ basis[j] - basis[j] @ basis[i]
            if np.linalg.norm(comm) > 1e-10 and is_independent(comm, basis):
                basis.append(comm / np.linalg.norm(comm.flatten()))
                changed = True

print(f"DLA dimension: {len(basis)} (expected 6)")
assert len(basis) == 6


DLA dimension: 6 (expected 6)




Code
# Verify parity commutation
P = np.kron(sz, sz)
for name, H in [('ZI', H1), ('IZ', H2), ('XX', H3)]:
    comm = P @ H - H @ P
    print(f"[P, {name}] = 0: {np.allclose(comm, 0)}")
    assert np.allclose(comm, 0)

print(f"\nParity P = ZZ commutes with all generators.")
print(f"DLA = 6 < dim su(4) = 15: symmetry-restricted.")


[P, ZI] = 0: True
[P, IZ] = 0: True
[P, XX] = 0: True

Parity P = ZZ commutes with all generators.
DLA = 6 < dim su(4) = 15: symmetry-restricted.






Closing the three Ising generators under commutation yields a six-dimensional algebra inside the fifteen-dimensional \(\mathfrak{su}(4)\). The gap is enforced by the \(\mathbb{Z}_2\) parity operator \(\sigma_z \otimes \sigma_z\), which commutes with every generator and blocks the nine missing directions.

title: Entanglement of a Parametric Two-Qubit State
text:
When two systems share a joint pure state, a measurement on one can be correlated with the other in ways no shared classical variable could reproduce. That excess correlation is entanglement, and in the pure-state case it has a clean signature. An observer holding only one of the two subsystems cannot see the global state and instead works with the reduced density matrix obtained by tracing out the partner. For a product state this reduced state is itself pure and the subsystem carries definite information of its own. Once the parts are entangled the reduced state turns mixed, and the more mixed it becomes, the more entanglement the pair holds.
Mixedness needs a number to track it. One choice is the purity, which equals one for a pure state and drops as the state spreads over more eigenvalues. Another is the von Neumann entropy, which is zero for a pure state and climbs toward its maximum as those eigenvalues even out. For a pair of qubits the reduced state has only two eigenvalues, so a single weight fixes both quantities at once.
The family \(\cos\theta\,|00\rangle + \sin\theta\,|11\rangle\) is already written in its Schmidt form, meaning the entanglement is laid bare by the two coefficients with no further diagonalization needed. The reduced density matrix is diagonal with eigenvalues \(\cos^2\theta\) and \(\sin^2\theta\), and its von Neumann entropy is the binary entropy of those weights, a single curve in the mixing angle. The ends \(\theta = 0\) and \(\theta = \pi/2\) put all the weight on one term and give product states, while \(\theta = \pi/4\) balances the two and produces a Bell state whose reduced density matrix is maximally mixed.
This exercise traces out one qubit, computes the purity and the von Neumann entropy across the family, and locates the separable and maximally entangled points.



Consider the parametric two-qubit state:
\[
|\psi(\theta)\rangle = \cos\theta\,|00\rangle + \sin\theta\,|11\rangle.
\]
(a) Compute the reduced density matrix \(\rho_A = \mathrm{Tr}_B(|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|)\).
(b) Compute the purity \(\gamma = \mathrm{Tr}(\rho_A^2)\) and the von Neumann entropy \(S = -\mathrm{Tr}(\rho_A \ln \rho_A)\) as functions of \(\theta\).
(c) Show the state is maximally entangled at \(\theta = \pi/4\) and separable at \(\theta = 0, \pi/2\).





The full density matrix is:
\[
|\psi\rangle\langle\psi| = \cos^2\!\theta\,|00\rangle\langle 00| + \sin^2\!\theta\,|11\rangle\langle 11| + \cos\theta\sin\theta\bigl(|00\rangle\langle 11| + |11\rangle\langle 00|\bigr).
\]
Tracing over subsystem \(B\): the partial trace acts on the second tensor factor. The diagonal terms survive since \(\langle 0|0\rangle = \langle 1|1\rangle = 1\). The off-diagonal terms vanish because \(\langle 0|1\rangle = 0\):
\[
\mathrm{Tr}_B(|00\rangle\langle 11|) = |0\rangle\langle 1| \cdot \underbrace{\langle 1|0\rangle}_{=\,0} = 0.
\]
Therefore:
\[
\boxed{\rho_A = \cos^2\!\theta\,|0\rangle\langle 0| + \sin^2\!\theta\,|1\rangle\langle 1| = \begin{pmatrix} \cos^2\!\theta & 0 \\ 0 & \sin^2\!\theta \end{pmatrix}.}
\]
The reduced state is diagonal in the computational basis, with eigenvalues \(\lambda_0 = \cos^2\!\theta\) and \(\lambda_1 = \sin^2\!\theta\).



Purity:
\[
\gamma = \mathrm{Tr}(\rho_A^2) = \cos^4\!\theta + \sin^4\!\theta.
\]
Using the identity \(\cos^4\!\theta + \sin^4\!\theta = 1 - 2\cos^2\!\theta\sin^2\!\theta = 1 - \frac{1}{2}\sin^2\!(2\theta)\):
\[
\gamma = 1 - \frac{1}{2}\sin^2(2\theta).
\]
Von Neumann entropy:
\[
S = -\cos^2\!\theta\,\ln(\cos^2\!\theta) - \sin^2\!\theta\,\ln(\sin^2\!\theta).
\]
This is the binary entropy function \(h(\cos^2\!\theta)\).



\(\theta = \pi/4\) (maximally entangled): \(\cos^2(\pi/4) = \sin^2(\pi/4) = 1/2\).
\[
\rho_A = \frac{I}{2}, \qquad \gamma = \frac{1}{2}, \qquad S = \ln 2.
\]
The reduced state is maximally mixed, one bit of entanglement. The state is the Bell state \((|00\rangle + |11\rangle)/\sqrt{2}\).
\(\theta = 0\) or \(\pi/2\) (separable): The state is \(|00\rangle\) or \(|11\rangle\), a product state.
\[
\rho_A = |0\rangle\langle 0| \text{ or } |1\rangle\langle 1|, \qquad \gamma = 1, \qquad S = 0.
\]
Zero entanglement. The purity is maximal (\(\gamma = 1\)), confirming the reduced state is pure, the hallmark of a product state.







Code
import sympy as sp

t = sp.Symbol('theta', real=True, positive=True)

lam0 = sp.cos(t)**2
lam1 = sp.sin(t)**2

# Purity
gamma = sp.trigsimp(lam0**2 + lam1**2)
print(f"γ = {gamma}")

# Entropy

title: Surjectivity of the Exponential Map on
text:
Time evolution in quantum mechanics is generated by Hermitian Hamiltonians, and the unitary operators that result are obtained by exponentiating them. If we strip out the factor of \(i\) and keep the bare generator, it is skew-Hermitian, meaning it equals minus its own conjugate transpose. These generators form the Lie algebra written \(\mathfrak{u}(D)\), and exponentiating any one of them lands inside the unitary group \(U(D)\). A natural question is whether the reverse also holds, so that every unitary can be written as the exponential of some generator.
For the unitary group the answer is yes, and this reflects the fact that \(U(D)\) is compact. Compactness is what makes the exponential map cover the whole group, and once it is dropped the property can fail. Over the real invertible matrices, for instance, exponentiating a real generator always produces a positive determinant, so no generator can ever reach a matrix whose determinant is negative.
The reason surjectivity holds is that a unitary is a normal operator, so the spectral theorem supplies an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors with eigenvalues of unit modulus, each of the form \(e^{i\theta}\). Collecting the phases \(\theta_j\) and weighting the corresponding eigenprojectors by them assembles a skew-Hermitian generator whose exponential reproduces the original unitary. Because each phase can be shifted by any multiple of \(2\pi\) without changing its eigenvalue, many different generators map to the same unitary, so the map covers the group while being far from one to one.
The notebook diagonalizes Haar-random unitaries and checks that exponentiating the principal-logarithm generator returns each matrix.



The exponential map \(\exp: \mathfrak{u}(D) \to U(D)\) connects the Lie algebra (infinitesimal generators) to the Lie group (finite unitaries). A crucial question: is every unitary \(U\) reachable as \(e^X\) for some generator \(X\)? For the unitary group the answer is yes, the exponential map is surjective. This is a special property of compact groups and fails for non-compact groups (e.g., \(\mathrm{GL}(n, \mathbb{R})\) contains matrices with negative determinant, unreachable from \(\exp\)).



Show that every \(U \in U(D)\) can be written as \(U = \exp(X)\) for some \(X \in \mathfrak{u}(D)\).





Since \(U\) is unitary, it is normal (\(UU^\dagger = U^\dagger U\)), so the spectral theorem gives:
\[
U = \sum_{j=1}^D e^{i\theta_j} |v_j\rangle\langle v_j|,
\]
where \(\{|v_j\rangle\}\) is an orthonormal eigenbasis and \(\theta_j \in (-\pi, \pi]\) are the eigenphases.



Define
\[
X = \sum_{j=1}^D i\theta_j\,|v_j\rangle\langle v_j|.
\]



\[
X^\dagger = \sum_j (-i\theta_j)|v_j\rangle\langle v_j| = -X. \quad \checkmark
\]
So \(X \in \mathfrak{u}(D)\).



The matrix exponential acts diagonally on the eigenbasis:
\[
\exp(X) = \sum_j \exp(i\theta_j)|v_j\rangle\langle v_j| = U. \quad \checkmark
\]



The map is not injective: \(X\) and \(X + 2\pi i\, |v_j\rangle\langle v_j|\) produce the same \(U\). The choice \(\theta_j \in (-\pi, \pi]\) selects the principal logarithm, but other branches exist. This multi-valuedness reflects the compactness of \(U(D)\).







Code
import sympy as sp
from sympy import Matrix, I, exp, pi, simplify, eye

# Verify exp map surjectivity for SU(2):
# exp(-i*theta*n.sigma/2) covers all of SU(2)
theta = sp.Symbol('theta', real=True)

# Example: R_z(theta) = exp(-i*theta*sigma_z/2)
sz = Matrix([[1, 0], [0, -1]])
# Explicit formula: diag(e^{-itheta/2}, e^{itheta/2})
Rz = Matrix([[sp.exp(-I*theta/2), 0], [0, sp.exp(I*theta/2)]])
print(f'R_z(theta) = {Rz}')

# Verify det = 1 (element of SU(2))
det = simplify(Rz.det())
print(f'det(R_z) = {det}')
assert det == 1, 'Not in SU(2)!'
print('det = 1 verified: R_z in SU(2)')

# Verify unitarity: R_z * R_z^dag = I
prod = simplify(Rz * Rz.adjoint())
print(f'R_z * R_z^dag = {prod}')
assert prod == eye(2)
print('Unitarity verified!')

# Period: R_z(4*pi) = I (double cover of SO(3))
Rz_4pi = Rz.subs(theta, 4*pi)
print(f'\nR_z(4pi) = {simplify(Rz_4pi)}')
print('SU(2) is the double cover of SO(3): period = 4pi')


R_z(theta) = Matrix([[exp(-I*theta/2), 0], [0, exp(I*theta/2)]])
det(R_z) = 1
det = 1 verified: R_z in SU(2)
R_z * R_z^dag = Matrix([[1, 0], [0, 1]])
Unitarity verified!

R_z(4pi) = Matrix([[1, 0], [0, 1]])
SU(2) is the double cover of SO(3): period = 4pi









Every \(U \in U(D)\) is the exponential of a skew-Hermitian generator, recovered by diagonalizing \(U\) and taking the principal logarithm of each eigenphase, so \(\exp\) maps \(\mathfrak{u}(D)\) onto all of \(U(D)\). The map is not injective, since shifting any eigenphase by \(2\pi\) leaves \(U\) unchanged.


Code
import numpy as np
from scipy.linalg import expm
from scipy.stats import unitary_group

np.random.seed(42)

for D in [2, 4, 8]:
    U = unitary_group.rvs(D)

    # Step 1: Diagonalize
    evals, evecs = np.linalg.eig(U)
    phases = np.angle(evals)  # θ_j ∈ (-π, π]

    # Step 2: Construct X = i Σ θ_j |v_j⟩⟨v_j|
    X = evecs @ np.diag(1j * phases) @ evecs.conj().T

    # Verify skew-Hermiticity
    assert np.allclose(X, -X.conj().T), "X is not skew-Hermitian!"

    # Verify exp(X) = U
    U_recovered = expm(X)
    err = np.linalg.norm(U_recovered - U)
    print(f"D={D}: ‖exp(X) − U‖ = {err:.2e}")
    assert err < 1e-10

print("\nSurjectivity verified: every Haar-random U = exp(X).")

D=4: ‖exp(X) − U‖ = 2.61e-15
D=8: ‖exp(X) − U‖ = 5.38e-15

title: Bloch Sphere Geodesics and the Fubini-Study Metric
text:
Two quantum states that differ only by an overall phase give identical predictions for every measurement, so that phase carries no physical content. The honest space of pure states is therefore not the Hilbert space itself but the set of rays that survive once the phase is divided out, the complex projective space. To do geometry there we need a notion of distance that ignores the phase, and the natural one starts from the overlap of two nearby states and keeps only the part of their difference that moves the ray, discarding the part that merely rotates the phase.
That construction is the Fubini-Study metric. The distance it assigns to two states is the angle \(\arccos|\langle\psi|\phi\rangle|\) between the rays they span, so states with large overlap sit close together and orthogonal states sit a quarter turn apart. Reading distance as an angle is more than a figure of speech, since the line element is literally the metric of a curved surface and the shortest paths are arcs along it.
The same line element measures how quickly a state moves under evolution, because a Hamiltonian pushes a state a definite distance per unit time in this geometry. It is the real part of the quantum geometric tensor, which is why it returns in quantum speed limits and in questions of how sensitively a state responds to a parameter. For a single qubit the space of rays is two-dimensional, and the metric works out to that of a round sphere, the familiar Bloch sphere, though it carries a radius that the bare Bloch vector does not make obvious.
This exercise derives the line element directly from the qubit state in the half-angle parametrization, reduces it to the metric of a sphere of radius one half, and measures the geodesic distance from the north pole to a point on the equator, both by integrating along the meridian and from the closed-form overlap formula.



A general single-qubit pure state is
\[
|\psi(\theta, \varphi)\rangle = \cos\frac{\theta}{2}|0\rangle + e^{i\varphi}\sin\frac{\theta}{2}|1\rangle.
\]
(a) Starting from the Fubini-Study line element \(ds^2_{\mathrm{FS}} = \langle d\psi|d\psi\rangle - |\langle\psi|d\psi\rangle|^2\), show that
\[
ds^2_{\mathrm{FS}} = \frac{1}{4}\bigl(d\theta^2 + \sin^2\!\theta\, d\varphi^2\bigr).
\]
(b) Compute the geodesic distance between \(|0\rangle\) (north pole) and \(|+\rangle = (|0\rangle + |1\rangle)/\sqrt{2}\) (equator).





Step 1: Compute \(|d\psi\rangle\).
Differentiating the state:
\[
|d\psi\rangle = -\frac{1}{2}\sin\frac{\theta}{2}\,d\theta\,|0\rangle + e^{i\varphi}\left[\frac{1}{2}\cos\frac{\theta}{2}\,d\theta + i\sin\frac{\theta}{2}\,d\varphi\right]|1\rangle.
\]
Step 2: Compute \(\langle d\psi|d\psi\rangle\) (Term 1).
The squared norm gives three contributions:
\[
\langle d\psi|d\psi\rangle = \frac{1}{4}\sin^2\frac{\theta}{2}\,d\theta^2 + \frac{1}{4}\cos^2\frac{\theta}{2}\,d\theta^2 + \sin^2\frac{\theta}{2}\,d\varphi^2.
\]
Using \(\sin^2 + \cos^2 = 1\):
\[
\langle d\psi|d\psi\rangle = \frac{1}{4}d\theta^2 + \sin^2\frac{\theta}{2}\,d\varphi^2.
\]
Step 3: Compute \(|\langle\psi|d\psi\rangle|^2\) (Term 2).
The inner product \(\langle\psi|d\psi\rangle\) has two contributions:

From \(d\theta\): \(\cos\frac{\theta}{2}\cdot(-\frac{1}{2}\sin\frac{\theta}{2}) + \sin\frac{\theta}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{2}\cos\frac{\theta}{2} = 0\). (The real part cancels!)
From \(d\varphi\): \(\sin\frac{\theta}{2}\cdot i\sin\frac{\theta}{2} = i\sin^2\frac{\theta}{2}\,d\varphi\).

Therefore:
\[
|\langle\psi|d\psi\rangle|^2 = \sin^4\frac{\theta}{2}\,d\varphi^2.
\]
Step 4: Combine.
\[
ds^2_{\mathrm{FS}} = \frac{1}{4}d\theta^2 + \sin^2\frac{\theta}{2}\,d\varphi^2 - \sin^4\frac{\theta}{2}\,d\varphi^2 = \frac{1}{4}d\theta^2 + \sin^2\frac{\theta}{2}\cos^2\frac{\theta}{2}\,d\varphi^2.
\]
Using \(\sin^2\frac{\theta}{2}\cos^2\frac{\theta}{2} = \frac{1}{4}\sin^2\theta\):
\[
\boxed{ds^2_{\mathrm{FS}} = \frac{1}{4}\bigl(d\theta^2 + \sin^2\!\theta\,d\varphi^2\bigr).}
\]
This is the metric of a round sphere of radius \(R = 1/2\). The Bloch sphere has half the radius of the “geographic” unit sphere, the factor \(1/2\) arises from the half-angle parametrization of \(\mathrm{SU}(2)\).



The north pole is \(\theta = 0\) and \(|+\rangle\) is at \(\theta = \pi/2\), \(\varphi = 0\). Along the meridian (\(d\varphi = 0\)), the geodesic length is:
\[
d_{\mathrm{FS}} = \int_0^{\pi/2} \frac{1}{2}\,d\theta = \frac{\pi}{4}.
\]
Equivalently, using the closed-form Fubini-Study distance:
\[
d_{\mathrm{FS}}(|\psi\rangle, |\phi\rangle) = \arccos|\langle\psi|\phi\rangle|.
\]
\[
|\langle 0|+\rangle| = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}, \qquad d_{\mathrm{FS}} = \arccos\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} = \frac{\pi}{4}. \quad \checkmark
\]







Code
import sympy as sp

t, p = sp.symbols('theta phi', real=True)

# Term 1: <dψ|dψ>
term1_dtheta = sp.Rational(1, 4)
term1_dphi = sp.sin(t/2)**2

# Term 2: |<ψ|dψ>|²
term2_dphi = sp.sin(t/2)**4

# FS metric coefficient for dφ²
g_phi = sp.trigsimp(term1_dphi - term2_dphi)
print(f"g_φφ = {g_phi}")
print(f"g_φφ = (1/4)sin²θ : {sp.trigsimp(g_phi - sp.sin(t)**2/4) == 0}")

# Geodesic distance
dist = sp.acos(1/sp.sqrt(2))
print(f"d_FS(|0⟩, |+⟩) = {dist} = {sp.nsimplify(dist)}")

g_φφ = (1/4)sin²θ : True

# Verify d_FS via the overlap formula for several pairs
ket0 = np.array([1, 0], dtype=complex)

The Fubini-Study line element is that of a round sphere of radius \(1/2\), and the geodesic distance equals \(\arccos|\langle\psi|\phi\rangle|\). For the qubit the geometry of states is exactly the geometry of that sphere, with the half-angle parametrization accounting for the radius.
